summary: Phil Hetzel leads solutions engineering at Braintrust, an agent quality platform that evaluates whether agents perform as expected in production and whether new versions can be trusted during experimentation. He contrasts traditional observability—focused on uptime, latency, and error codes via tools like Grafana and Datadog—with agent observability, which faces three core problems. First, agents are non-deterministic, requiring broader qualitative metrics such as groundedness in retrieved context, expected tool usage, and alignment to brand standards. Second, agent traces are extremely large and complex: semi-structured with large volumes of unstructured text, sometimes over a gigabyte per trace with individual spans reaching 20 megabytes, yet still needing real-time visibility. Braintrust built a custom database from the ground up after finding ClickHouse insufficient for text-based indexing, incorporating a write-ahead log for instant trace visibility, analytical indexes for fast filtering, and a forked version of Tantivy—a Rust-based full-text search library similar to Apache Lucene. Third, the persona using observability shifts from systems engineers to non-technical domain experts—clinicians, nurses, wealth advisors, lawyers—who review traces and provide feedback. Braintrust treats observability and evals as the same problem, differing only in that evals run in batch with known inputs while observability runs in real time with unknown inputs. Human annotation is central: experts grade agents and justify their reasoning, and those justifications are processed by LLMs to create scalable scoring functions that identify failure modes for automated scoring. The platform recently added topic modeling via embedding and clustering on traces to surface user intent, sentiment, and recurring issues. Braintrust positions itself as providing functional observability of agent quality, with technical metrics like duration, time to first token, and cache hits coming along automatically.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Speaker Introduction and Braintrust Overview
sections.summary: Phil Hetzel introduces himself as leading solutions engineering at Braintrust, with 12 years in consulting including leading the global Databricks practice at Slalom. He joined Braintrust after noticing customers struggled to move generative AI proofs of concept to production. Braintrust is an agent quality platform focused on production confidence and experimentation confidence.

sections.title: Traditional Observability Scope
sections.summary: Traditional observability is established and focuses on uptime and technical performance—latency, error codes, duration—using tools like Grafana and Datadog. Braintrust itself uses Datadog for monitoring 400/500 errors on their website. Building blocks include metrics, traces, and spans, which also apply to agent observability.

sections.title: Problem 1: Non-Determinism and Broader Metrics
sections.summary: Agents are non-deterministic unlike traditional deterministic applications with known control flows. Agent observability must measure both traditional-flavored metrics (time to first token, total tokens, duration) and qualitative metrics: groundedness in retrieved context, expected tool usage, and brand alignment from system prompts. These require far larger trace information than traditional observability handles.

sections.title: Problem 2: Trace Data Challenges and Custom Database
sections.summary: Agent traces are semi-structured with large unstructured text volumes, can exceed one gigabyte, with individual spans reaching 20 megabytes, and must arrive in real time. Braintrust needs simultaneous fast ingest-and-read workflows and SQL-based analytical querying. They built a custom database with a write-ahead log for instant visibility, analytical indexes for fast filtering, and a forked Tantivy index (Rust-based, similar to Apache Lucene) for full-text search across traces, unified through a SQL-like language.

sections.title: Problem 3: Shifting User Personas
sections.summary: Traditional observability serves technical personas—systems and product engineers. Agent observability involves non-technical domain experts: clinicians, registered nurses, wealth advisors, and lawyers who are closest to users or the problem space. They can write prompts in natural language, review traces, and contribute real value to agent improvement—a workflow absent from traditional observability.

sections.title: Observability and Evals as One Problem; Future Direction
sections.summary: Hetzel explains that Braintrust treats observability and evals as the same problem—the only difference is that evals run in batch with known inputs while observability runs in real time with unknown inputs. He discusses the future direction: Braintrust recently rolled out topic modeling in their SaaS offering, running lightweight LLMs to perform embedding and clustering on traces to surface user intent, sentiment, and recurring issues, shortening the iteration loop between production problems and experimental fixes.

sections.title: Q&A: Functional Observability, Human Annotation, and Database Rationale
sections.summary: In Q&A, Hetzel clarifies that Braintrust provides functional observability focused on agent quality, while technical metrics like duration, time to first token, and cache hits come along automatically. He explains human annotation: experts grade agents and justify their reasoning; those justifications are processed by LLMs to create scalable scoring functions that identify failure modes for automated scoring. On the custom database, he reveals Braintrust previously used ClickHouse but moved away because it could not handle text-based indexing needed for agent traces; the founder, an early SingleStore employee, built the custom system. Traced data can be added to offline datasets for experimentation. The platform distinguishes between online scoring of known unknowns and open-ended insight derivation for unknown unknowns.
